intrinsic_value_estimate: About $60-70 per share, central about $70. Method: 1987 owner earnings of about $2.25/share (range $2.07-2.47), calculated as net income $916.1M plus depreciation and amortization $153.5M minus capex of $151.9M-$299.6M, on 372M shares. Grown at 8-10% a year for 10 years, then 5%, discounted at 10% (Coca-Cola's own borrowing cost, about 10%; the packet has no Treasury yield). The full range runs from about $42 (8% growth, 12% rate) to about $81 (12% growth, 10% rate). The framework's literal net-working-capital test gives about $0.05/share and fails, but per brk-letter-1987#18 and brk-letter-1981#3 it does not apply to a franchise business.
margin_of_safety: At $46.56 the stock is about 22-33% below the central value of $60-70. The margin disappears (-11% to +5%) only if growth slows to about 8% and the rate is 12%. There is no margin on net working capital. The safety comes mainly from how durable and predictable the franchise's earnings are, not from the balance sheet. The owner-earnings yield of about 4.8% is below Coca-Cola's roughly 10% debt cost, but at 8-10% growth owner earnings reach 10% of today's price in about 8-10 years.

key_reasons.reason: The business earns high returns on equity without needing leverage
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: Return on average equity was 19.7-21.2% in 1977-1981, when total debt was 3.5-9.3% of capital. Soft-drink operating income of $1,432.5M on $4,174M of identifiable assets in 1987 is about 34% pretax (ar-1987 note 16). Reported ROE of 27.2% in 1987 is partly helped by leverage, so the underlying figure is about 20%.

key_reasons.reason: A durable trademark-and-distribution moat that survived the company's own mistake
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: 44% of world soft-drink volume, twice the nearest competitor; US fountain share 59%, more than 2-to-1; gross margin on concentrate to US bottlers about 63%. After the 1985 formula change, Coca-Cola classic became the top US soft drink in 1986, and the company's sugar-cola volume grew 5% while competitors grew 1% (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The business needs little capital, so most earnings are available to owners
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Owner earnings (brk-letter-1986); Berkshire criteria 2, 3 and 5 (brk-letter-1982, brk-letter-1986#10)
key_reasons.evidence: 1987 soft-drink capex was $170M against $1.43B of segment operating income. Total capex fell from $412M to $346M to $300M over 1985-87 while depreciation was about $152M. Owner earnings are about $770-918M, or $2.07-2.47 per share.

key_reasons.reason: There is room for long growth within the moat
key_reasons.framework_principle: Valuation: buy a business whose price makes sense 'even should the future develop much along the lines of its past' (brk-letter-1981#3, brk-letter-1987#18)
key_reasons.evidence: International per-capita consumption was 16% of the US rate in 1986. US servings rose from 203 in 1980 to 274 in 1987. Continuing EPS grew from $0.84 (1977) to $2.43 (1987), about 11% a year, with no down year.

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have created far more than $1 of market value per $1 retained
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: About $1.7-2.0B was retained over 1982-87, while market value rose from about $4.3B (end-1981) to about $17.3B now, even after $1.43B of buybacks and the CPE spin-off. Continuing income rose by about $484M a year.

key_reasons.reason: Able management is in place, focused on the core business and returning capital
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Honest, able management in place; buybacks below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: Goizueta and Keough have led since 1981. Entertainment was spun into the 49%-owned CPE, and plastics, pasta and South Africa were exited. 1984-85 buybacks of 33.4M shares were made at about $18-25, or 12-15x earnings. A 40M-share program is authorized through 1990, and the dividend payout is being cut toward 40% so more is reinvested.

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible, not cheap, against a central value of about $70, which justifies a large but not maximum position
key_reasons.framework_principle: 7. Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965); 6. No catalyst needed (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is about 19.2x 1987 EPS and about 21x owner earnings. The central value of $60-70 gives a 22-33% margin, but stress cases ($42-49) leave none, and the price is near the 52-week high of $49.12. No 1988 results are in the packet.

risks: The valuation depends heavily on value after year 10 (55-70% of the total). If growth slows to about 8% and money is valued at 12%, the stock is fairly valued or overvalued.

Reported growth is flattered by currency: key currencies rose 27% (1986) and 16% (1987) against the dollar, and about 77% of soft-drink operating income is international. A stronger dollar would cut reported earnings.
Rising leverage: gross debt to capital was 45.6% at end-1987, buybacks are funded with short-term debt, and management has raised its net debt ceiling to 35%.
Capital may again go into low-return assets outside the core: past entertainment acquisitions, Embassy bought with stock in 1985, CCE earning about 5.8% on equity, continuing bottler stakes.

The US is a two-company advertising contest: US soft-drink operating margin was about 15%, against about 27% internationally. Formula-priced syrup contracts with most US bottlers limit domestic pricing power.
Foods is a low-moat, commodity-exposed business (orange solids) that took a $36M restructuring charge in 1987.
Reporting is promotional, and gains from selling stakes in subsidiaries ($67M in 1985, $375M in 1986, $40M in 1987) flow into earnings.
Missing data: no 1988 results, no long-term bond yield, no local-currency growth, no split of capex into maintenance and growth.
what_would_change_my_mind: 1988 results showing flat or falling local-currency unit volume or soft-drink operating income, meaning past growth was mostly currency and price.
Evidence that the main competitor is closing the US fountain or food-store share gap, or that concentrate prices cannot keep up with inflation.
A large acquisition outside soft drinks, especially one paid for in stock, or debt rising toward the 35% ceiling for anything other than buybacks clearly below value.
Buybacks continuing at prices above my estimate of intrinsic value, or a dilutive share issuance.
Owner earnings coming in at the low end ($2.07) with maintenance capex close to total capex, which would push value toward $50-55.
A price at or above about $65-70 would remove the margin for further buying; a fall toward $35-40 (the 1988 range) would justify going toward the 40% maximum.
sell_triggers: The intended holding period is permanent, like the three permanent holdings (brk-letter-1987#18). Do not sell because the price rises or because of market forecasts.

Sell if the economics of the franchise erode lastingly, e.g. sustained loss of world or US share, or return on equity falling toward ordinary levels (about 15%) without leverage, meaning the business was misread (brk-letter-1987#18 notes that exiting a marketable holding is easier than exiting a controlled business).

Sell or trim if management repeatedly misallocates capital: large value-destroying diversification, share issuance for weak assets, or leverage that threatens permanent loss of capital (bpl-letter-1967-oct).
Sell if reporting loses candor, e.g. aggressive accounting that hides deteriorating core results (brk-letter-1983#2).
Reconsider only if the price runs so far above intrinsic value that a clearly superior use of capital exists. This is secondary to the permanent-holding default.
